case_prompt: Meridian Coffee is a fictional 60-store coffee chain in the UK. Same-store revenue grew 4% last year, but store-level profit fell 12%. Management wants to understand the main profit drivers before deciding whether to change prices, staffing, or the menu. In this Tutorial session, first build a structure for the problem; we will then practise the supporting case math. All company names and figures are fictional.

transcript.content: Meridian Coffee is a fictional 60-store coffee chain in the UK. Same-store revenue grew 4% last year, but store-level profit fell 12%. Management wants to understand the main profit drivers before deciding whether to change prices, staffing, or the menu. In this Tutorial session, first build a structure for the problem; we will then practise the supporting case math. All company names and figures are fictional.
I'd look at market, customer and competition.
What is the client actually trying to fix, and what is profit computed from? Use those two questions to rebuild the first level.
The client wants to restore profit, so I would start with profit equals revenue minus cost. I would split revenue into price and volume, then split volume into footfall and conversion.
Assistance changed from Guided to Assisted after the first successful retry.
A store serves 18,000 transactions per month at an average ticket of £6.50. What is monthly revenue?
I will multiply 18,000 by 6.5. That is 117,000—I'm not sure whether I should express that per store or for the whole chain.
Write down the unit of the answer you are trying to produce before you calculate again.
The target is revenue per store per month. Transactions per store per month multiplied by pounds per transaction gives £117,000 per store per month.
The candidate requested no further hints; Independent practice began.
Without hints, structure the volume side for a coffee store and tell me where you would start.
I would split volume into footfall, conversion, purchase frequency and seat productivity. I would start with footfall because I want to separate a demand problem from an in-store execution problem.

independence_marker.note: You asked for no more hints from this point on.

headline.learning_summary: You can now do the first-level profit breakdown and the per-store revenue calculation unaided, and you stopped needing hints from the third rep onward. What has not settled yet: after listing branches you do not say which one you would look at first, or why.

dimensions.name: Problem Structuring
dimensions.evidence: First-level breakdown is now reliable; second-level branches still default to generic buckets.

dimensions.name: Quantitative Skills
dimensions.evidence: All three calculations completed unaided, with units stated before computing.

dimensions.name: Business Judgment & Insight
dimensions.evidence: Needed a prompt each time before asking what a finding meant for the client.

dimensions.name: Communication
dimensions.evidence: Clear delivery; occasionally explains the method before stating the answer.

recurring_mistakes.label: Branches listed without a priority
recurring_mistakes.note: Three of four structuring reps. The branches keep improving; “where do I start” is never answered.

recurring_mistakes.label: Numbers read without asking what they mean
recurring_mistakes.note: Both attempts to interpret a figure stopped at describing it.

independent: First-level breakdown of profit = revenue − cost
Fixing the unit of the answer before calculating
needs_help: Industry-specific second-level structure (needs the scope narrowed first)

next_priorities.title: Ordering the structure
next_priorities.current: Produces sensible branches, never states a starting point.
next_priorities.target: After any structure, say “I would start with X, because Y” unprompted.
next_priorities.drill: Five structuring reps. Rule: branches are not finished until one is chosen and justified; delete any branch you cannot justify.
next_priorities.assistance: Hints if you stall for the first two; fully unaided for the last three.

next_priorities.title: From a number to its meaning
next_priorities.current: Reads figures accurately, rarely says what they imply for the client.
next_priorities.target: Complete observation → why → implication → what to check next, unaided.
next_priorities.drill: Five exhibit reps, all four steps each time.
next_priorities.assistance: Hints if you stall for the first two, unaided thereafter.

strength.headline: You fix the unit of the answer before you calculate
strength.detail: On the first attempt you produced 117,000 and could not say what it meant. Once prompted, you wrote down “pounds per store per month”, worked backwards to the inputs, and got both the number and the unit right. That habit will prevent most calculation errors you would otherwise make.

priority.headline: You can produce branches, but never say which one comes first
priority.detail: In three of four structuring reps you stopped at listing branches. A structure exists to decide what to investigate next; one that cannot be ordered cannot move a real case forward.

next_step.headline: Name the first branch and the reason, every time
next_step.detail: Next session, five structuring reps under one rule: after the branches, add “I would start with X, because Y”. Delete any branch you cannot justify — if you cannot justify it, it usually did not belong there.

annotations.headline: This is a general framework, not a structure for this case
annotations.comment: None of market, customer or competition answers “why did profit fall”. The client asked about profit, and profit has an explicit formula — that formula is where the structure should start.
annotations.improvement: For any problem, first ask how the metric the client cares about is computed, then break down that formula.

annotations.comment: You were not handed branches here, only two questions to rebuild from. Structuring has to be built rather than received, so a worked answer would have taught nothing.

annotations.headline: Rebuilt from the profit formula — the right move
annotations.comment: Starting from profit = revenue − cost and splitting revenue into price and volume is correct, and you did it on the second attempt without further help.
annotations.improvement: The cost side is still empty though. Store profit fell 12% while revenue rose, which points at cost — that branch deserved priority.

annotations.comment: The branches are listed but not ordered. Revenue up 4% with profit down 12% already points at cost or mix, which is enough to choose a starting point out loud.
The arithmetic is right, but you calculated before deciding what the number would represent, so afterwards you could not say whether it was one store or the chain.

annotations.headline: Unit first, inputs second
annotations.comment: Once you wrote “pounds per store per month” the required inputs became obvious and the answer was right first time. This is the habit most worth keeping from this session.

annotations.headline: Branches specific to a coffee store, with no hint
annotations.comment: Footfall, conversion, purchase frequency and seat productivity are the real volume drivers for this format, not a generic template — and you gave a starting point with a reason unprompted.
annotations.improvement: Note the scope: the coach had already narrowed this to the volume side. Building a full structure from nothing is still untested.

takeaways: Build the structure from the formula behind the metric the client asked about, not from a framework you memorised.
A structure is not finished until the branches are ordered — an unordered structure cannot move the analysis.
Write down the unit of the answer first and the calculation path usually appears.
